paragraphs.source_en: This time, the one who leapt into the bath was unlike the usual monsters: he was a man with a patterned tattoo on his back. His back seemed meant to depict the tale of Iwami Jutaro brandishing a great sword and slaying a serpent; unfortunately, the tattoo was not yet finished, so one could not tell where the python was. Thus Mr. Jutaro of the tattoo looked somewhat disappointed. As he jumped into the bath, he said, “This water is damned hot.” Then another man jumped in after him and said, “This is really... it ought to be a little cooler...” It was plain that, because the bathwater was too hot, he was baring his teeth and grimacing. When he met the fellow with the Jutaro design face to face, he greeted him: “Why, boss, is that you?” The fellow with Jutaro on his back replied, “Oh, it’s you!” Then he asked, “How has things been with Tami lately?” “How has he been? Well, he is carrying on with tremendous gusto, anyway.” “He can’t always keep throwing himself into it like that...” “That’s true! That fellow has a crooked disposition... for some reason, no one likes him. I don’t know what the matter really is, but people just don’t trust him much. A craftsman cannot be like that.” “Exactly. A man like Tami does not know how to be humble and pleasant; he is always holding his head too high, and that is why people do not trust him.” “That is true. He is forever thinking his own skill is so extraordinary, and in the end he only hurts himself!” “All the old-timers in Shirogane Street have died off. Nowadays, the only ones who can be called bosses are old Gen from the bucket shop, the boss at the brick-and-tile shop, and you yourself. A man like me was born and bred here, but as for people like Tami, who knows where they crawled out from?” “Just so. Still, it is something that he managed to get as far as he has.” “Yes. For some reason, he simply does not win people’s liking. He does not mix with people.” From beginning to end, the two of them did nothing but speak ill of Tami.

paragraphs.source_en: So much for the bath on this side, dirty as a fire cistern; now look over at the bath where the white medicinal water is clouding the surface. Why, it is packed beyond capacity. Rather than say that people are soaking in the bathwater, it would be more accurate to say that a little water has been poured in among the people. And yet these people are entirely at their leisure; people only squeeze in, and not a single one goes out. Seeing so many people soaking in it, and knowing that the water was changed only once a week, I thought admiringly, “No wonder the water is so filthy.” I looked more carefully at everyone in the bath and discovered that Mr. Kushami was squeezed into the left-hand corner, crouching there with his face boiled bright red. I thought, poor man, if only someone would make a space and let him get out; but no one moved, and my master himself showed no sign of coming out. He merely stayed motionless, his skin reddened by the heat. This was no easy feat. Perhaps, from the desire not to waste so much as possible of the two sen five rin he had paid for his bath, he could not bear to come out even after soaking until his whole body turned red. But I, a cat devoted to my master, could not help worrying for him from the window frame: if he did not get out soon, he would faint in there. Just then, next to my master, a bather with his whole body immersed frowned and said, “This water is rather too hot; the heat up my spine feels a bit like needles pricking me.” In saying this, he was secretly seeking the sympathy of the assembled monsters. Then someone cried out proudly, “Not at all! It is just right, neither too cool nor too hot. A medicinal bath will not work unless it is like this. In my home province, we bathe in water twice as hot as this.” A fellow with a folded towel set on his head asked everyone, “What disease is this medicinal bath actually good for?” “It works for every sort of ailment, they say. It is good for anything at all. That is splendid!” The man who said this was a fellow with a lean face that, in both color and shape, resembled a yellow cucumber. If this medicinal bath were truly so effective, he ought already to have grown at least a little sturdier. Another know-it-all type offered his opinion: “After the medicine has been freshly changed, the third or fourth day is when it works best, so today is just the right time to bathe.” When I looked at the man, he turned out to be flabbily bloated. “Would it work if one drank some?” This was a delicate, affected voice, and I could not see who had spoken. Someone or other answered, “If you drink a cup after it has cooled and then go to bed, strangely enough you will not have to get up to urinate at all. You might try it.”

paragraphs.source_zh: 关于这边的像消防水缸一般肮脏的浴池，就说到这，你再看看那边泛着白色药水的浴池吧。嚄，这还真是超满员哪。与其说是浴池的水里泡着人，还不如说在人里倒进点水更为恰当。不过，这些人倒都是悠悠闲闲，只有挤进来，却无一人要出去的。这么多人进来泡着，再加上一个星期才更换一次水，我感叹地想：“难怪水这么脏了。”我又仔仔细细地看了一下浴池中所有的人，原来苦沙弥先生被挤在左角上，蹲在那里，烫得满脸通红。我想，怪可怜的，如果有人让出个空当儿，让他出来就好了，可是谁都不动，主人也没有要出来的迹象。只是皮肤烫得红红的，一动不动。这可不是个容易做到的事儿。大概他是出于尽可能不要白花这两分五厘的洗澡钱的心理，所以才这样泡得全身通红也舍不得出来的吧。可是，我这个对主人忠心耿耿的猫儿，在窗子框上不由得替主人担心起来，不快些出来会晕倒在里边的。这时，在主人旁边有一个把整个身子都泡在水里的浴客，他皱着眉头说：“这水可是有点烫啦，后脊梁热得有点像针扎似的。”他说这话，暗中在寻求各位怪物的同情。于是，有的人自鸣得意地嚷道：“哪里！正好不凉不热。药浴不这样是起不了作用的。在我老家，我们洗的水比这儿还要热上一倍呢。”一个把叠起的浴巾顶到头上的家伙问大伙：“这个药浴究竟是管什么病的？”“什么病痛都管事儿，说是管百病的嘛。真够意思！”说这样话的，是一位面孔瘦削、在色形上都像线黄瓜似的老兄。如果这药浴真是那样管用，他早就该多少变得结实一点啦。又有一个万事通式的人物发表意见说：“换一次药水后，第三天或第四天药才最管用，所以今天洗最是时候。”我一看这人，原来是个虚胖子。“喝点也能管用吗？”这是一个娇里娇气的声音，看不清说话的人是谁。又不知是谁回答说：“凉了以后喝上一杯，然后睡觉，就完全不用起来撒尿啦，您可以试试嘛。”
